objectives.text: Justify the within-subjects design with counterbalanced order and a one-week gap, and the choice of backward rather than forward digit span.
Interpret the paired-samples t-test result, t(23) = 2.41, p = .024, d = 0.49, including why normality of difference scores was checked.
Evaluate how lack of blinding, a single task and an underpowered sample limit the conclusions, and propose design changes addressing each.

questions.prompt: In your study, you chose backward rather than forward digit span. What was the main reason for this choice?
options: Reversing digits requires active manipulation, so it taps the central executive
Backward span is less affected by practice across the two sessions
Backward span mainly measures storage, which sleep loss is known to disrupt
Backward span is longer, so it avoids ceiling effects after normal sleep
questions.explanation: You argued that reversing a sequence requires active manipulation, relying on the central executive, which sleep loss may particularly affect. It is forward span that mainly measures storage, which is why you noted that without it you cannot separate manipulation from storage.

questions.prompt: Your study tested each participant in both sleep conditions, in counterbalanced order, at least one week apart. Which statements correctly justify these design features?
options: Counterbalancing spreads practice effects equally across the two conditions
Counterbalancing stops participants knowing which condition they are in
Comparing each person with themselves removes individual differences in baseline span
The one-week gap allowed recovery so restriction did not carry over
A within-subjects design means sleep duration need not be measured
The one-week gap removes any practice effect on the second session
questions.explanation: Testing everyone twice controls individual differences, counterbalancing balances order effects, and the week gap allowed recovery. Counterbalancing does not blind participants; you noted they knew their condition. The gap prevents carry-over of restriction but cannot remove practice effects, which counterbalancing handles instead.

questions.prompt: In your study, half the participants did the restricted night first. If everyone had done the normal night first, what problem would arise?
options: Restriction effects would carry over into the normal-sleep session
Actigraphy would be unable to confirm the sleep manipulation
Participants could no longer be compared with themselves across conditions
Practice on the span task would be confounded with the sleep condition
questions.explanation: With a fixed order, any improvement from practice would always fall in the second (restricted) session, confounding order with condition. Carry-over from restriction would not arise here, because restriction would come second, and your one-week gap addressed carry-over separately.

questions.prompt: Your paired-samples t-test gave t(23) = 2.41, p = .024, d = 0.49. Which statements correctly interpret this result or your normality check?
options: If sleep had no effect, a difference this large would occur about 2.4% of the time
Normality was checked on each condition's raw scores separately, as the test requires
Normality was checked on difference scores because the paired t-test analyses those differences
The 23 degrees of freedom reflect 24 pairs of scores minus one
There is a 2.4% probability that restricted sleep has no effect on span
A d of 0.49 means restriction lowered span by about half a digit
questions.explanation: A paired t-test works on each participant's difference score, so normality of those differences matters, and df = n − 1 pairs. The p-value is the probability of data this extreme if the null is true, not the probability the null is true; d is in SD units, not digits.

questions.prompt: In your study, the Shapiro–Wilk test on difference scores gave p = .31. What did this result tell you about your analysis?
options: The sleep effect was not significant once normality was taken into account
The differences showed no significant departure from normality, so a paired t-test was appropriate
The differences were significantly non-normal, so a non-parametric test was needed
The two conditions had equal variances, so a paired t-test was appropriate
questions.explanation: A non-significant Shapiro–Wilk result (p = .31) means the difference scores did not depart significantly from normality, supporting the paired t-test, which analyses those differences. It tests normality, not equality of variances, and says nothing about the sleep effect itself.

questions.prompt: Your paired t-test compared span after normal and restricted sleep. Which statements about this analysis and its interpretation are accurate?
options: The significant result confirms the study had at least 80% power for this effect
Pairing scores within participants reduces error variance compared with an independent-groups test
The effect size describes the mean difference relative to the variability of the difference scores
A non-significant Shapiro–Wilk result proves the difference scores are perfectly normal
A p of .024 shows the effect is large enough to matter in everyday life
The test works on each participant's difference between conditions, not the two sets of raw scores
questions.explanation: A paired t-test analyses within-person differences, which removes individual differences in baseline span and so reduces error, and d scales the mean difference by their variability. A small p shows the result is unlikely under chance, not that it matters practically. Shapiro–Wilk cannot prove normality, and you noted power was below 80%.

questions.prompt: You noted that participants knew their condition, so expectations may have reduced effort. Which design change would best address this limitation?
options: Telling participants their actual sleep was longer or shorter than it was
Measuring motivation and including a placebo-style partial sleep condition
Recruiting enough participants to detect an effect of d = 0.49
Adding a forward digit span task alongside the backward span task
questions.explanation: Expectation effects arise because participants know they slept little; measuring motivation and comparing against a condition whose expected effects are matched separates sleep from expectation. Adding forward span addresses the single-task limitation, and a larger sample addresses power, not blinding.

questions.prompt: Your discussion identifies several limitations. Which statements correctly describe what these limitations mean for your conclusions?
options: Actigraphy confirming the manipulation rules out reduced effort as an explanation
Because the result was significant, being underpowered for d = 0.49 does not affect your conclusions
Higher sleepiness ratings cannot separate a genuine sleep effect from participants' expectations
Without forward span, the deficit cannot be attributed specifically to manipulation rather than storage
Counterbalancing order removes the influence of participants' expectations about tiredness
Lower power for the observed effect means your estimate of its size is imprecise
questions.explanation: A single backward task cannot isolate manipulation, self-rated sleepiness fits both sleep and expectation accounts, and lower power makes d = 0.49 imprecise. Significance does not cancel low power, and neither counterbalancing nor actigraphy addresses participants knowing their condition.

questions.prompt: Your observed effect was d = 0.49, but your study was powered for d = 0.6. Which design change would best address this limitation in a replication?
options: Switch to an independent-groups design to remove practice effects
Raise the alpha level to .10 so the effect is easier to detect
Base a new power analysis on d = 0.49 and recruit more participants
Keep 24 participants but add forward span as a second outcome
questions.explanation: Detecting a smaller effect with 80% power needs a larger sample, so you would base the power analysis on d = 0.49 and recruit more people. Switching to independent groups would lose the error reduction from pairing and lower power further. Raising alpha only trades power for more false positives.
